title: Mystical visions: strange sightings at Bristol photo festival – in pictures
excerpt: From women floating across the shore to magical patches of Irish land, this year’s exhibitions are full of fantastic yet confounding photography

From women floating across the shore to magical patches of Irish land, this year’s exhibitions are full of fantastic yet confounding photography

Thu 5 Nov 2026 02.00 ESTLast modified on Thu 5 Nov 2026 09.04 EST
content_text: From women floating across the shore to magical patches of Irish land, this year’s exhibitions are full of fantastic yet confounding photography‘Fluid landscapes’ … Akshay Mahajan, People of Clay, 2022 Photograph: Akshay MahajanThu 5 Nov 2026 02.00 ESTLast modified on Thu 5 Nov 2026 09.04 ESTLiu Hsing Yu, My father & motherIn Family Times, Liu Hsing Yu and Annie Wang explore how family relationships are continually reshaped by time, memory, care and social change. In this image, Liu recreates his parents’ wedding photograph with their roles reversed, using performance and family history to reflect on identity, belonging and Taiwan’s changing attitudes towards gender and sexuality. Family Times is at Centrespace Gallery, Bristol, until 11 November. In collaboration with Ministry of Culture, Republic of China (Taiwan). All shows are a part of Bristol photo festivalPhotograph: Liu Hsing YuAnnie Wang, The Mother as a CreatorIn The Mother as a Creator, Wang photographs herself and her son each year, layering past and present into a visual time tunnel that reveals motherhood as an evolving relationship. Together, the works show family as something constantly remade through ritual, repetition and carePhotograph: Annie WangJulián Barón, The Magic LabyrinthMarking the 90th anniversary of the Spanish civil war, No Pasarán brings together three artists and researchers exploring history, memory and resistance. Julián Barón shows how the war is remembered, employing historical reenactments and the fading inscriptions left by Republican militia on the walls of an abandoned barracks. No Pasarán by Anna Jornet, Julián Barón and Natasha Christia is at Redcliffe Caves, Bristol, until 15 November. In collaboration with Institut Ramon Llull, Acción Cultural Española and Insitituto CervantesPhotograph: Julián BarónGeorge Hallett, Mongezi Feza (musician) and friend at home, London, 1973South African photographer George Hallett (1942–2020) documented everyday life, cultural identity and resistance throughout apartheid and exile, himself living in exile in Europe from 1970 to the mid-1990s. This exhibition includes portraits of exiled South African activists, visual artists and jazz musicians. George Hallett: Home and Exile is at IC Visual Lab, Bristol until 15 November. In collaboration with Liverpool John Moores UniversityPhotograph: Courtesy George Hallett Research CollectionKjell-Åke Andersson, Bargoed Colliery, Wales, 1973-76Dark Tales explores the relationship between the gothic and British documentary photography. Drawing primarily from the Martin Parr Foundation Collection, the exhibition brings together celebrated and lesser-known works depicting postwar Britain to the present through waning industries, unsettling domestic scenes and shadowy nocturnal landscapes. Dark Tales: British Documentary Photography and the Gothic is at Martin Parr Foundation, Bristol, until 20 December. In collaboration with Martin Parr Foundation. See more in our galleryPhotograph: Kjell-Åke AnderssonMaria Lax, from the series Stray Sod Drawing on accounts from the Irish National Folklore Collection, Maria Lax explores enchanted patches of earth believed to disorient those who step upon them, leading them into unfamiliar worlds. The work reflects on moments of uncertainty and transformation, connecting traditional stories of becoming lost with the destabilising effects of grief, political change and rapid technological shifts in contemporary life. Stray Sod by Maria Lax at the Welcome Building, Bristol, until 15 November. In collaboration with Frame | Contemporary, Art FinlandPhotograph: Maria LaxMichel Campeau, from the series DarkroomMichel Campeau documents photographic darkrooms as they disappear in the wake of digital photography. Shot with a digital camera and direct flash, the series avoids nostalgia, instead revealing the worn surfaces, improvised repairs and handwritten notes that bear witness to the tactile processes of analogue printing. Darkroom by Michel Campeau is at Arnos Vale Cemetery, Bristol, until 20 December. In collaboration with Martin Parr FoundationPhotograph: Michel CampeauPhotos by Kegham Djeghalian SrFounded in Gaza in 1944 by Armenian genocide survivor Kegham Djeghalian Sr, Photo Kegham was the city’s first commercial photography studio, documenting everyday Palestinian life through decades of upheaval. Although much of the archive has been lost, three surviving boxes of photographs, now cared for by his grandson Kegham Djeghalian Jr, preserve a rare visual history of Gaza. Photo Kegham by Kegham Djeghalian Jr is at Albion Dockside, Bristol, until 15 December. In collaboration with Photopia (Cairo, Egypt), supported by the British CouncilPhotograph: Courtesy of Kegham Djeghalian Jr.Joy Gregory, Stockwell Siren from the series Celebrity Blonde, 2003 performance Catching Flies With Honey is the first major survey of Joy Gregory’s work. Through photography, film, installation and textiles, Gregory explores identity, history, race and beauty, using processes from Victorian photographic techniques to digital media to examine how power shapes societies and collective memory. Joy Gregory: Catching Flies With Honey is at Arnolfini, Bristol, until 7 February 2027. Exhibition originated by Whitechapel GalleryPhotograph: Joy GregoryHolly Lynton, from the series Beyond the BoundsFor more than 15 years, Holly Lynton has explored the intersections of faith, history, labour and landscape across rural communities in the US. Beyond the Bounds examines places shaped by spiritual awakenings, from towns founded by psychics to former sites of religious revival. Beyond the Bounds by Holly Lynton is at Bristol Cathedral until 11 November. In collaboration with Bristol Cathedral, Spectrum and HAPAXPhotograph: Holly LyntonAkshay Mahajan, People of Clay Akshay Mahajan’s People of Clay traces hidden histories along the Brahmaputra River, exploring the stories, myths and memories of communities divided by colonial borders. Through photography, collage and found materials, Mahajan creates a subjective cartography shaped by listening, observation and engagement. People of Clay by Akshay Mahajan is at Bristol Museum and Art Gallery until 14 February. In collaboration with Bristol Museum & Art Galleries, Friends of BMAG and ArtFundPhotograph: Akshay MahajanAkshay Mahajan, People of Clay, 2022 Drawing on local folklore, the work reimagines forgotten narratives and challenges official histories, revealing memory as something constantly transformed and retold. People of Clay becomes an act of remembrance, reflecting on identity, belonging and the fluid landscapes we inheritPhotograph: Akshay MahajanSheida Soleimani, from the series Persistence StudiesPersistence Studies takes its title from avian ecology, where the term describes research into how long birds remain within a landscape before disappearing. Focusing on European starlings and house sparrows, the exhibition explores shifting ideas of nativeness, invasion and belonging. These birds are considered invasive in one place while declining in another. Persistence Studies is at Bristol Museum & Art Gallery until 14 February 2027. In collaboration with Brigstow Institute and Bristol Museum and Art Galleries Photograph: Sheida Solemani.Untitled (Rashid Mahdi, left), c. 1955 Questioning conventional histories of photography, this exhibition challenges the familiar narrative centred on figures such as Nicéphore Niépce and William Henry Fox Talbot. Instead, it proposes that photography’s history is multiple, shaped as much by exclusion as inclusion. One of Many: An Alternative History of Photography is at Albion Dockside, Bristol, until 15 November. In collaboration with the French Institute in the UKPhotograph: Claude Germain/Musée du quai Branly–Jacques Chirac, Paris
